content.title: About
content.content: Chicken liver is an internal organ of the bird, rich in nutrients. It has a soft texture, a slightly bitter taste, and is commonly used in dishes across many world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken liver is one of the cheapest sources of high‑quality protein.
In many traditional cuisines it is prepared as pâtés, fried pieces, or added to soups.
The liver accumulates vitamins and minerals, giving it a higher nutritional value than most muscle meats.
Its iron content exceeds that of beef liver.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and preventing anemia.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Liver contains B12, B2, B6, which are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and especially beneficial during pregnancy.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Liver protein is highly digestible and supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: High vitamin A levels
items.content: Excessive intake can cause hypervitaminosis A, particularly in children and pregnant women.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: The liver can accumulate toxins and heavy metals, so choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to liver.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Liver contains a notable amount of cholesterol, so people with hypercholesterolemia should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken liver can be sautéed, stewed, baked, or made into pâté. Before cooking, rinse it, remove any visible vessels, and cut into bite‑size pieces. It pairs well with onion, garlic, apples, and various spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh chicken liver in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C in an airtight container for no more than 1–2 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check the smell—any sour or off odor indicates spoilage.
